newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK jobless queues to shrink in December.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK jobless queues to shrink in December.

text.p: Unemployment in Britain is expected to have fallen again in December although somewhat less spectacularly than in November.
A Reuter poll of economists found a consensus forecast that Britain's jobless queues were reduced by 30,000 last month, following a record drop of 96,000 the month before.

Economists warned that new initiatives such as the jobseekers allowance (JSA) and the benefit fraud hotline may be exaggerating the decline in unemployment, but few doubted that job creation was accelerating as the economy picks up.
The figures will be released at 0930 GMT on Wednesday.

"The impact of the jobseekers allowance thus far has been to backlog claimants, which exaggerated November's record declines by at least 20,000," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

The JSA replaced old-style unemployment benefit in October and requires claimants to provide additional evidence that they are actively seeking work. The switchover has caused backlogged claims to mount up.
The fraud hotline was launched in August and by November had received more than 100,000 calls concerning people suspectd of claiming benefit while working at the same time.
That further muddied the waters when trying to measure the trend in unemployment, Barr said.
Philip Uglow, economist at Union Plc, said hiring of temporary workers in the run-up to Christmas had also helped to massage down the jobless figures.
"However, despite special factors pushing unemployment lower recently, the trend rate of decline has certainly quickened as the economy has gathered pace," he said.
Barr estimated the trend rate of decline in unemployment at abot 40,000 each month, well above the 15-20,000 seen through most of last year.

But any immediate fears that the British economy is reaching its natural rate of unemployment, below which inflation will take off, should be assuaged by average earnings and unit wage costs data, released alongside the jobless figures.

Economists forecast annualised average earnings growth unchanged at 4.0 percent in November. Unit wage costs are expected to fall to 4.3 percent in the three months to November compared with a year earlier, from 4.6 in October.

"It is only a matter of time before average earnings growth rises further...given the tightness of the labour market," Barr said. "However, we do not expect a move this month. The January-April pay rounds may prove the trigger for a renewed increase."
He noted service sector earnings growth has jumped to four percent, having loitered at 2.75 percent in November 1995.

David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders, agreed further cuts in unemployment were inevitable. "With vacancies at job centres at record levels, there can be little doubt that the labour market is tightening."
Job centre vacancies rose to nearly 270,000 in November, a rise of 77,700 over the year.
